title: Route Parameters and Constraints in ASP.NET Core
description: Master route parameters, optional values, custom constraints, and catchall segments for flexible URL handling.

data.text: What Are Route Parameters?

Route parameters are placeholders in a route pattern that capture values from the URL. When a request matches a route, ASP.NET Core extracts the parameter values and passes them to the action method — either as matching parameters or through `RouteData.Values`.

terms.definition: A placeholder in a route template like {id} that captures a value from the URL.
A parameter marked with ? that is not required for the route to match.
A condition that restricts what values a route parameter can accept, like {id:int}.
A *catchall segment that captures all remaining URL parts as one string.

data.caption: How route parameters are extracted from a URL and passed to an action.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[URL: /products/42] --> B{Pattern: products/{id:int}}
    B -->|Match| C[id = 42]
    C --> D[ProductsController.GetById(42)]
    B -->|No Match| E[404 Not Found]

data.text: Reading Parameters from the URL
The simplest way to read a route parameter is to add a method parameter with the same name as the route placeholder:

data.title: Route parameter via action parameter
data.content: The id from the URL is automatically passed to the action parameter.

data.title: Action receiving a route parameter
data.content: ASP.NET Core automatically converts the URL value to the parameter type.

data.text: Visiting `/Products/Details/42` calls `Details(42)`. ASP.NET Core automatically converts the string `42` to an `int`. This automatic conversion is part of **model binding**.
Reading Parameters via RouteData
You can also read route values directly from the `RouteData.Values` dictionary. This is useful for custom segments that do not match an action parameter name:

data.title: Reading a custom segment from RouteData
data.content: Access any route value by its segment name.

data.text: `RouteData.Values` returns objects. Cast them to the correct type when reading values that are not strings.
Optional Route Parameters

Add a `?` after a segment name to make it optional. The route will still match when that segment is missing from the URL. Optional parameters are `null` for reference types and the default value for value types:

data.title: Optional parameter in a route
data.content: Both /Home/Check and /Home/Check/42 will match this route.

data.title: Handling an optional parameter in an action
data.content: Use the null-coalescing operator to provide a fallback value.

data.text: Route Constraints
Route constraints restrict what values a parameter can match. They prevent ambiguous routes and return 404 early when a URL does not fit the expected pattern.

data.title: Applying multiple constraints
data.content: Combine a type constraint with a minimum value.
data.code:
app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "products",
    pattern: "Products/{id:int:min(1)}",
    defaults: new { controller = "Products", action = "Details" });

data.title: Constraint Order Matters
data.text: Constraints are evaluated left to right. If the first constraint fails, the route is rejected immediately. Put the most restrictive constraint first.
The Catchall Wildcard

The `*catchall` segment captures any remaining URL segments as a single string. It must always be the last segment in the pattern. This is useful for documentation sites, wiki pages, or catch-all error handling:

data.title: Catchall route pattern
data.content: Capture everything after the action into one parameter.

data.title: Using catchall in an action
data.content: Accept the catchall parameter as a string.

data.text: Custom Route Constraints
When built-in constraints are not enough, you can create custom constraints by implementing `IRouteConstraint`. This is useful for validating parameters against a database or a business rule:

data.title: Custom route constraint example
data.content: A constraint that only allows even numbers for the id parameter.

data.title: When to Use Custom Constraints
data.text: Use custom constraints when a value depends on external data (e.g., checking if a product ID exists in the database) or when a business rule is too complex for a regex.
Attribute Routing with Parameters
Attribute routing supports all the same parameter features as convention-based routing, including optional parameters, constraints, and catchall:

data.title: Attribute route with optional parameter and constraint
data.content: Combine parameters, constraints, and optional values in one route.

data.title: Practice: Build a Blog Post Route
data.description: Create a PostsController with attribute routing that supports: GET /api/posts (all posts), GET /api/posts/{year}/{month}/{slug}, and GET /api/posts/archive/{*path}. Add constraints so that year must be a 4-digit number, month must be between 1 and 12, and slug must contain only lowercase letters and hyphens.
steps: Add Archive action with a catchall parameter.
Create an in-memory list of posts and return them from GetAll.
Test each route in the browser.
data.expectedOutcome: You will be able to design precise attribute routes with multiple constraints and a catchall segment.

items.text: Route parameters use {name} syntax in the route pattern.
items.hint: The placeholder name must match the action parameter name.

items.text: Add ? after a segment to make it optional.
items.hint: Optional parameters are null for reference types.

items.text: Use constraints like :int, :min(1), :regex(...) to restrict values.
items.hint: Constraints return 404 instead of calling the wrong action.

items.text: Use *catchall only as the last segment to capture long paths.
items.hint: There can be only one catchall per route.

items.text: You can read route values from RouteData.Values if needed.
items.hint: Action parameters are simpler when names match.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Route parameters capture values from the URL using {name} placeholders.
Optional parameters use the ? suffix and are null when missing.
Constraints like :int and :min(1) make routes safer and more precise.
The *catchall segment captures all remaining URL parts.
Attribute routing supports the same parameter features as convention-based routing.
data.takeaway: Route parameters and constraints give you precise control over which URLs your actions accept. Combine them to build clean, self-documenting routes.
